title: Unifying Themes of Life Science
seo_title: Grade 11 General Science: Unifying Themes of Life Science Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_code: Grade 11 General Science, Term 2: Chemistry and life science
standard_text: Unifying themes of life science: the characteristics of life, levels of organization, structure and function, homeostasis, energy and matter in living systems, and evolution and the unity and diversity of life. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 2)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 2): characteristics of life, levels of organization, homeostasis, classification and evolution. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: All living things are made of cells.
key_sub: Evolution explains the unity and diversity of life.
body_html:
How to think about it

All living things share characteristics: they are made of cells, use energy, grow and develop, respond to their environment, keep a stable internal environment (homeostasis), reproduce, and adapt over generations. Life is organized from atoms and molecules to cells, tissues, organs, organisms, populations, communities and ecosystems.

Structure fits function at every level. Energy flows and matter cycles through living systems. Evolution by natural selection explains why living things share features (unity) and also differ so much (diversity).

Example

Which is the smallest unit of life?

Not an atom

Answer: the cell

Example

Keeping body temperature at 37 °C is an example of?

Stable inside

Answer: homeostasis

Common mistakes

  • Thinking viruses are cells.
  • Thinking homeostasis means no change at all.
  • Thinking evolution is goal-directed.

faq.q: Why are viruses not usually called living?
faq.a: They are not made of cells and can reproduce only inside host cells.

faq.q: Why are there so many kinds of living things?
faq.a: Over millions of years, natural selection adapted populations to different environments.

items.q: In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below order?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below class?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 2, species B 5, species C 12. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
What is the common name of Mangifera indica?
items.e: Mangifera indica: mango.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 10, species B 12, species C 2. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
A quadrat survey found: species An 8, species B 20, species C 8. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below family?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: A quadrat survey found: species A 3, species B 12, species C 8, species D 3. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σn(n − 1)/N(N − 1).
Which is a property of living things but NOT of non-living things?
items.e: Mountains and crystals can grow from outside.

items.q: What is the common name of Triticum aestivum?
items.e: Triticum aestivum: wheat.

items.q: What is the common name of Panthera tigris?
items.e: Panthera tigris: tiger.

items.q: Why is growth not a defining property of living things?
c: non-living things such as mountains and crystals can also grow by accumulation
items.e: Growth in living things is from inside.

items.q: Which is the basic unit of classification?
items.e: Members can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

items.q: What is a taxon?
c: a group of organisms at any level of the hierarchy
items.e: e.g. the genus Panthera is a taxon.

items.q: Which is the scientific name for rice?
items.e: Oryza sativa: rice.

items.q: In the hierarchy of classification, which taxon comes directly below phylum?
items.e: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

items.q: How should a scientific name be written when printed?
c: in italics, genus with a capital letter and species epithet in small letters
with both words capitalized in plain type
items.e: e.g. Mangifera indica.

items.q: Why is reproduction not a defining property of living things?
c: some living organisms, such as mules and worker bees, cannot reproduce
items.e: Metabolism and cellular organization are defining.

items.q: Which is the scientific name for wheat?
items.e: Triticum aestivum: wheat.

items.q: Which is the scientific name for human?
items.e: Homo sapiens: human.

items.q: Which organ system does the liver belong to?
items.e: The liver is part of the digestive system.

items.q: Which level is the largest?
items.e: An organism is made of all its systems.

items.q: Which level of organization is a skin cell?
items.e: A skin cell is a cell.

items.q: Which organ system does the thyroid gland belong to?
items.e: The thyroid gland is part of the endocrine system.

items.q: Which list goes from smallest to largest?
c: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
tissue → cell → organ → organ system → organism
cell → organ → tissue → organ system → organism
cell → tissue → organ system → organ → organism
items.e: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems.

items.q: Which organ system does the lungs belong to?
items.e: The lungs is part of the respiratory system.

items.q: Which organ system does the small intestine belong to?
items.e: The small intestine is part of the digestive system.

items.q: What level is made of many cells working together?
items.e: Many cells make up a tissue.

items.q: Which level of organization is the nervous system?
items.e: The nervous system is an organ system.

items.q: Mark reads about a body system that collects information and sends messages that control the body. Which system is it?
items.e: The nervous system collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: Which level of organization is the lining of the stomach?
items.e: The lining of the stomach is a tissue.

items.q: Which organ system does the white blood cells belong to?
items.e: The white blood cells is part of the immune system.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for breathing faster when you run?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Which organ system does the bladder belong to?
items.e: The bladder is part of the excretory (urinary) system.

items.q: Which level of organization is a lung?
items.e: A lung is an organ.

items.q: Kevin reads about a body system that moves the body by pulling on bones. Which system is it?
items.e: The muscular system moves the body by pulling on bones.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for getting oxygen to muscle cells?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Kenneth reads about a body system that breaks food down into nutrients the body can use. Which system is it?
items.e: The digestive system breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.

items.q: Which two systems work together most directly for fighting an infection carried in the blood?
items.e: Systems interact to keep the body working.

items.q: Which organ system does the heart belong to?
items.e: The heart is part of the circulatory system.

items.q: What does ADH do?
c: makes the kidneys filter more blood
makes the collecting duct more permeable to water
causes more urine to be made
items.e: It acts through aquaporins.

items.q: The kidneys filter 130 cm³ of blood plasma per minute and produce 1.2 cm³ of urine per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
When the metabolic rate increases, which is the body responding to?
items.e: More respiration releases more heat.

items.q: What is a taxis?
c: a change in the rate of movement only
a directional movement of a whole organism towards or away from a stimulus
items.e: Kinesis is a non-directional change in speed or turning.

items.q: Diane's body temperature is 37.6 °C (normal is about 37 °C). What does the body do?
c: sweating and blood vessels in the skin widen
shivering and blood vessels in the skin narrow
items.e: Negative feedback moves it back toward 37 °C.

items.q: When shivering starts, which is the body responding to?
items.e: Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.

items.q: How does it help body temperature control when arterioles in the skin constrict (vasoconstriction)?
c: Less heat is lost by evaporation.
More blood flows near the skin surface, so more heat is lost by radiation.
Less blood flows near the skin surface, so less heat is lost.
Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.
items.e: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and controls these responses.

items.q: Jasmine's body temperature is 35.7 °C. The body shivers. Why?
c: to make heat and warm up
to lose heat and cool down
items.e: The response opposes the change.

items.q: An impulse travels 20 mm along an axon in 2.0 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
How does insulin lower blood glucose?
c: it is broken down into glucose
it makes the kidneys excrete glucose
it increases glucose uptake by cells and activates glycogenesis
items.e: More glucose channel proteins appear in membranes.

items.q: Rafael's body temperature is 36.1 °C (normal is about 37 °C). What does the body do?
c: shivering and blood vessels in the skin narrow
sweating and blood vessels in the skin widen
items.e: Negative feedback moves it back toward 37 °C.

items.q: How does it help body temperature control when sweating increases?
c: Water in sweat evaporates, taking heat (latent heat) from the skin.
Less heat is lost by evaporation.
Less blood flows near the skin surface, so less heat is lost.
Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.
items.e: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and controls these responses.

items.q: Insulin released after a meal is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: How does it help body temperature control when the metabolic rate increases?
c: Water in sweat evaporates, taking heat (latent heat) from the skin.
Less blood flows near the skin surface, so less heat is lost.
Less heat is lost by evaporation.
items.e: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and controls these responses.

items.q: How does it help body temperature control when arterioles in the skin dilate (vasodilation)?
c: Less heat is lost by evaporation.
Less blood flows near the skin surface, so less heat is lost.
More blood flows near the skin surface, so more heat is lost by radiation.
Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.
items.e: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and controls these responses.

items.q: Dennis's body temperature is 37.6 °C. The body sweats. Why?
c: to make heat and warm up
to lose heat and cool down
items.e: The response opposes the change.

items.q: The refractory period of a neurone is 0.80 ms. Calculate the maximum frequency of impulses, in impulses per second.
items.e: Maximum frequency = 1 ÷ 8.00 × 10−4 s = 1,250 Hz.

items.q: Platelets calling more platelets to a cut until it clots is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: What is homeostasis?
c: changing body temperature with the weather
keeping the internal environment within restricted limits
items.e: For example core temperature, blood glucose and water potential.

items.q: The kidneys filter 130 cm³ of blood plasma per minute and produce 0.50 cm³ of urine per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
Which kingdom has members that are euglenoids, with a pellicle and a flagellum?
items.e: Euglena photosynthesizes in light.

items.q: What is a flora?
c: a store of pressed, dried and labeled plant specimens on sheets
a place where wild animals are kept in protected surroundings like their natural habitat
a tool that identifies organisms using pairs of contrasting characters
an account of the plant species found in an area
items.e: flora: an account of the plant species found in an area.

items.q: Which taxonomic aid is a collection of preserved plant and animal specimens?
items.e: museum: a collection of preserved plant and animal specimens.

items.q: Which taxonomic aid is an account of the plant species found in an area?
items.e: flora: an account of the plant species found in an area.

items.q: Which kingdom has members that are prokaryotic, mostly unicellular, with a cell wall of peptidoglycan?
items.e: Monera: prokaryotic, mostly unicellular, with a cell wall of peptidoglycan.

items.q: Which taxonomic aid is a place where wild animals are kept in protected surroundings like their natural habitat?
items.e: zoological park: a place where wild animals are kept in protected surroundings like their natural habitat.

items.q: Why are fungi called saprophytes?
c: they absorb food from dead and decaying matter
items.e: They are important decomposers.

items.q: Which description fits kingdom Animalia?
c: prokaryotic, mostly unicellular, with a cell wall of peptidoglycan
multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that ingest food
multicellular eukaryotes with a cellulose cell wall that make their own food
items.e: Animalia: multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that ingest food.

items.q: What is the cell wall of diatoms made of?
items.e: Their deposits form diatomaceous earth.

items.q: Which kingdom has members that are heterotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall of chitin?
items.e: Fungi: heterotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall of chitin.

items.q: What is a zoological park?
c: a place where wild animals are kept in protected surroundings like their natural habitat
a garden of living plants grown and labeled for study
an account of the plant species found in an area
items.e: zoological park: a place where wild animals are kept in protected surroundings like their natural habitat.

items.q: Which kingdom has members that are unicellular eukaryotes?
items.e: Protista: unicellular eukaryotes.

items.q: Which kingdom has members that are multicellular eukaryotes with a cellulose cell wall that make their own food?
items.e: Plantae: multicellular eukaryotes with a cellulose cell wall that make their own food.

items.q: What are heterocysts in cyanobacteria used for?
items.e: e.g. Nostoc and Anabaena.

items.q: What is a lichen?
c: a symbiotic association of an alga and a fungus
items.e: They are pollution indicators.

items.q: What is the genetic material of bacteriophages usually?
items.e: Plant viruses usually have single-stranded RNA.

items.q: What are prions?
c: abnormally folded proteins that cause disease
items.e: e.g. mad cow disease (BSE).

items.q: Which description fits kingdom Fungi?
c: multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that ingest food
multicellular eukaryotes with a cellulose cell wall that make their own food
prokaryotic, mostly unicellular, with a cell wall of peptidoglycan
heterotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall of chitin
items.e: Fungi: heterotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall of chitin.

items.q: Which kingdom has members that are multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that ingest food?
items.e: Animalia: multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that ingest food.

items.q: Which description fits kingdom Plantae?
c: heterotrophic eukaryotes with a cell wall of chitin
multicellular eukaryotes with a cellulose cell wall that make their own food
multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall that ingest food
items.e: Plantae: multicellular eukaryotes with a cellulose cell wall that make their own food.

items.q: Scientists compare a bat wing and a bee wing. They do the same job but are built very differently. What does this suggest?
c: The two species share a recent common ancestor.
They evolved separately in similar environments.
items.e: Analogous structures come from similar needs, not shared ancestry.
